section.title: The Lord of All Creation
section.sectionRationale: One of the great creation hymns of the Psalter, this psalm is a companion to Psalm 103's hymn of redemption. It stands within Book IV, Psalms 90 to 106, which answers Book III's crisis over the apparent failure of the Davidic covenant by returning to the eternal kingship and creative power of the LORD Himself. Structured as a meditation that follows the days of Genesis 1, from light and sky to land, creatures, and human labor, it turns the creation account itself into personal praise.
section.thesis: The LORD who wraps Himself in light, founds the earth, and waters every valley sustains all His creatures moment by moment from His open hand, and by His Spirit continually renews the face of the ground, so that the fitting end of such a world is not human self-sufficiency but a lifetime of praise.
section.frameNote: Six movements: praise to the majestic Creator, verses 1 to 4; the earth's foundations and the flood's appointed boundary, verses 5 to 9; provision for every living creature, verses 10 to 18; sun, moon, and the rhythm of labor, verses 19 to 23; the wide sea and the sustaining Spirit, verses 24 to 30; and a closing doxology with a vow of lifelong praise, verses 31 to 35.

units.label: Bless the LORD, O my soul

verses.text: Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, You are very great; You are clothed with splendor and {{hadar|majesty}}.
He wraps Himself in light as with a garment; He stretches out the heavens like a tent,
laying the beams of His chambers in the waters above, making the clouds His chariot, walking on the wings of the wind.
He makes the winds His messengers, flames of fire His servants.

units.label: He set the earth on its foundations
units.note: the earth's stability and the flood's appointed boundary

verses.text: He set the earth on its foundations, never to be moved.
You covered it with the deep like a garment; the waters stood above the mountains.
At Your rebuke the waters fled; at the sound of Your thunder they hurried away,
the mountains rose and the valleys sank to the place You assigned for them,
You set a boundary they cannot cross, that they may never again cover the earth.

units.label: He waters the mountains from His chambers

verses.text: He sends forth springs in the valleys; they flow between the mountains.
They give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst.
The birds of the air nest beside the springs; they sing among the branches.
He waters the mountains from His chambers; the earth is satisfied by the fruit of His works.
He makes the grass grow for the livestock and provides crops for man to cultivate, bringing forth food from the earth:
wine that gladdens the heart of man, oil that makes his face to shine, and bread that sustains his heart.
The trees of the LORD have their fill, the cedars of Lebanon that He planted,
where the birds build their nests; the stork makes her home in the cypresses.
The high mountains are for the wild goats, the cliffs a refuge for the rock badgers.

units.label: He made the moon to mark the seasons
units.note: sun, moon, and the rhythm of labor

verses.text: He made the moon to mark the seasons; the sun knows when to set.
You bring darkness, and it becomes night, when all the beasts of the forest prowl.
The young lions roar for their prey and seek their food from God.
The sun rises, and they withdraw; they lie down in their dens.
Man goes forth to his work and to his labor until evening.

units.label: How many are Your works, O LORD
units.note: the wide sea and the sustaining Spirit

verses.text: How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all; the earth is full of Your creatures.
Here is the sea, vast and wide, teeming with creatures beyond number, living things both great and small.
There the ships pass, and {{leviathan|Leviathan}}, which You formed to frolic there.
All creatures look to You to give them their food in due season.
When You give it to them, they gather it up; when You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good things.
When You hide Your face, they are terrified; when You take away their breath, they die and return to dust.
When You send Your {{ruach|Spirit}}, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth.

units.label: Bless the LORD, O my soul
units.note: doxology and a vow of lifelong praise

verses.text: May the glory of the LORD endure forever; may the LORD rejoice in His works.
He looks on the earth, and it trembles; He touches the mountains, and they smolder.
I will sing to the LORD all my life; I will sing praise to my God while I have my being.
May my meditation be pleasing to Him, for I rejoice in the LORD.
May sinners vanish from the earth and the wicked be no more. Bless the LORD, O my soul. Hallelujah!

hadar.gloss: Splendor, majesty, honor. Paired with hod, splendor, in verse 1, it pictures the LORD arrayed as a king in the very radiance and order of creation itself.

leviathan.gloss: A great sea creature, feared in the myths of Israel's neighbors as a chaos monster. The psalm strips away the terror, Leviathan is simply a creature the LORD formed to frolic in the sea He rules, compare Job 41.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. The same Spirit who hovered over the waters in Genesis 1:2 continually creates and renews the face of the ground; life itself is sustained breath by breath from God alone.

basic.context: This psalm is a hymn of praise that walks through creation the way Genesis 1 does, light and sky, land and water, plants and creatures, sun and moon, and finally man at his labor. It is not abstract theology but a personal act of worship, the psalmist stirring his own soul to bless the LORD for a world he still finds astonishing.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes God's ongoing sustaining care, not merely His past act of creation. Every creature depends on Him moment by moment, verse 27 to 30, and the whole psalm calls the reader to the same response the psalmist models, wonder that turns into praise rather than into pride at human mastery over nature.
basic.originalLanguages: God is clothed with hadar, majesty, verse 1, the very dress of a king. The Spirit, ruach, verse 30, is the same breath that hovered over creation in Genesis 1:2 and that continually renews the ground. Even Leviathan, livyatan, verse 26, feared elsewhere as chaos itself, is simply God's plaything in a sea He fully rules.
basic.typology: The winds and flames who serve as God's messengers, verse 4, are cited in Hebrews 1:7 as part of the case for the Son's supremacy over the angels. The renewing Spirit, verse 30, anticipates the Spirit's work of new birth and the future renewal of all creation.
basic.christ: Colossians 1:16-17 says all things were created through Christ and for Him, and in Him all things hold together, the fullest statement of what this psalm pictures in God's sustaining hand. Hebrews 1:7 quotes verse 4 directly to show that the Son who made the angels His servants is worshipped, not merely served by, the created order.
basic.god: God is shown as majestic Creator and patient Sustainer together, He who founded the earth and set the sea's boundary, and who still opens His hand every day so that every creature, without exception, is fed. His pleasure in His own works, verse 31, shows a God who delights in what He has made.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1 supplies the days of creation that this psalm turns into praise. Hebrews 1:7 quotes verse 4 concerning the Son's supremacy over angels. Colossians 1:16-17 states what this psalm pictures, that all things hold together in Christ. Romans 8:19-22 speaks of creation's longing for the very renewal this psalm attributes to God's Spirit.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's hymn to the Creator who sustains every creature and renews the face of the ground by His Spirit finds its fulfillment in Christ, through whom and for whom all things were made and in whom all things hold together, and in the Spirit who will one day renew not just the ground but the whole creation.

context.literary:
The psalm is a long journey through the world, but the route is not accidental. It loosely follows the order of Genesis 1: light and the stretched out heavens (verses 1 to 4), the waters gathered from the land (verses 5 to 9; compare Genesis 1:9-10), springs, grass and trees for the beasts and for man (verses 10 to 18; Genesis 1:11-13), sun and moon marking seasons (verses 19 to 23; Genesis 1:14-19), the sea with its living things (verses 24 to 26; Genesis 1:20-22), and God's rejoicing in His works (verse 31, echoing Genesis 1:31 and 2:2). The order is not rigid, since land animals appear well before the sea, but a reader who knows Genesis hears it everywhere. The difference is the grammar. Genesis tells a finished sequence in past tense; the psalm keeps slipping into the present, so that creation becomes a thing God is doing now.

The address of the psalm keeps shifting. Verses 1 to 4 and 10 to 18 talk about God in the third person, 'He wraps Himself,' 'He sends forth springs,' while verses 6 to 9 and 19 to 30 speak directly to Him, 'You covered it,' 'You bring darkness.' The psalm moves in and out of the praise like a person who cannot decide whether to describe the LORD or to speak to Him, and in the end does both.

There are signs of careful balance. Verses 19 to 23 set night against day, with the lions roaring at night and man going out to work in the morning; verses 10 to 13 and 14 to 18 move between water and what water grows. Verse 24 stands near the center as the psalm's exclamation, 'How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all,' and verses 27 to 30 turn the whole picture into a table at which all creatures wait to be fed.

The frame is the same as Psalm 103: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul' at the beginning and again at the end. The last word is 'Hallelujah,' which appears here for the first time in the Psalter, and it follows the one sour note, verse 35, as if the praise cannot be complete until the wicked are gone.
context.historical:
There is no heading, so the psalm gives no author or occasion. The Greek Old Testament attributes it to David, and tradition has often followed that, but the text is silent. What the psalm shows is a world seen through an ancient Israelite's eyes. Water is life and also danger, rain comes from above and springs from below, the cedars of Lebanon are famous, ships cross a sea that Israel never owned, and every creature, from the wild goat on the cliff to the stork in the cypress, has a fixed place.

Readers have long noticed that the psalm resembles the Egyptian Hymn to the Aten, a hymn from the fourteenth century BC addressed to the sun disc, especially in passages about night falling on the lions and morning sending men to work. The similarity may reflect shared ancient ideas about the world, or Israelite poets borrowing familiar images. The difference is what matters. The Egyptian hymn praises the sun itself; the psalm makes the sun and moon creatures who 'know' their appointed times (verse 19), and who work for the LORD who made them. The sun here is a servant, not a god.

Behind the verses on the waters lies the ancient picture of a world in which the sea was a threat. In the myths of Israel's neighbours the sea was a rival deity that the gods had to defeat. Psalm 104 uses the same imagery, the waters standing above the mountains, fleeing at a rebuke, hurrying away at the thunder, but gives the sea no will. It runs where it is told and stays where it is put. Even Leviathan, which Psalm 74:14 and Isaiah 27:1 associate with the dragons of the deep, is here a creature the LORD 'formed to frolic' in the sea. The first hearers, who knew what the sea could do, were being told that it is in the hands of their God.

The agricultural triad of wine, oil and bread in verse 15 was the basic produce of the land. Together with rain and the cycle of seasons, it described what Israel depended on, and what the covenant promised, Deuteronomy 11:14.
context.canonical:
Psalm 104 is one of the great creation texts of the Bible, set beside Genesis 1 and 2, Job 38 to 41, Psalm 33:6-9, Psalm 148 and Proverbs 8. It is also the nearest thing the Old Testament has to a poetic commentary on Genesis 1. Where Genesis says God separated the waters, the psalm shows them fleeing at His voice; where Genesis says He gave plants for food (Genesis 1:29-30), the psalm shows the springs and the cedars and the animals that depend on them. Job 38:8-11 and Jeremiah 5:22 speak of the boundary set for the sea, the same idea as verse 9, and Psalm 145:15-16 uses the same words as verses 27 and 28: 'The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season. You open Your hand.'

In the Psalter it follows Psalm 103 and shares its opening call, 'Bless the LORD, O my soul.' Psalm 103 had celebrated the God who forgives; Psalm 104 celebrates the God who makes. The two together hold redemption and creation in one praise. The next psalms, 105 and 106, retell Israel's history, so the sequence moves from the world, to the people in it, to their failures.

The New Testament takes the psalm in several directions. Hebrews 1:7 quotes verse 4 in its Greek form to say that angels are servants, while the Son is God. Acts 17:24-28 echoes verses 27 to 30, with God giving 'everyone life and breath and everything else,' and Jesus speaks in the same spirit when He points to the birds that the Father feeds, Matthew 6:26. Colossians 1:16-17 and John 1:3 say that the Creator the psalm praises made everything through the Son. Paul's picture in Romans 8:19-22 of creation waiting to be set free belongs to the same world, and Revelation 21:1 resolves the story with a new heaven and earth. Verse 30's 'You renew the face of the earth' also stands close behind Paul's phrase in Titus 3:5, 'renewal by the Holy Spirit.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wanted Israel to see the ordinary world as full of God. The rain, the grass, the lions at dusk, the sailor on the sea were not neutral facts; they were gifts handed out each day from one open hand. In an age when neighbouring peoples worshipped the sun, the storm and the sea, he insisted that all of them are works, with a Maker who delights in them and will outlast them.

He also meant his hearers to feel their place in it. People are mentioned briefly, once as farmers (verse 14), once as workers (verse 23), once as sailors by implication (verse 26), and they stand among the other creatures, equally dependent. Israel would have heard a gentle humbling. The one who can plough and sail and make wine still waits on God for breath (verses 29 and 30).

Last, he meant the poem to end in worship, not in observation. 'I will sing to the LORD all my life' (verse 33) is the response he hopes for, and 'May my meditation be pleasing to Him' is a prayer that his own reflection might be worth hearing. The psalm is an act of thought directed to God, and it wants hearers to join it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes creation in poetry and in the language of the senses. It speaks of God laying the beams of His chambers on the waters, of the earth being set on foundations, of the sun knowing when to set. These are not scientific claims about how the cosmos is built. The poet is painting what the world looks like from the ground, in images, just as we say that the sun rises. Treating verses 5 or 6 as a physics lecture would misuse them, and treating them as myth would ignore their sober claim that God made and keeps the world.

What the psalm clearly teaches is dependence. Verses 27 to 30 do not describe a one time act; they describe the way every creature lives, receiving food in season, from an open hand. That is a truth that applies to every reader. The psalm also gives a clear instruction to the reader: sing, meditate, rejoice, bless the LORD. As for verse 35, the wish that sinners vanish, it records the writer's longing for a world without evil rather than a command for believers to wish harm on anyone, and it needs to be read alongside Jesus' command to love our enemies, Matthew 5:44.

debates.question: What does verse 4 say about winds, flames and angels?

views.label: God makes the winds His messengers and flames His servants
views.case: The BSB takes the winds and flames as what God puts to work. The surrounding lines are about nature, clouds, wind and light. The verse then says that even the forces of storm do God's errands, which fits the psalm's claim that nothing in nature acts on its own.

views.label: God makes His angels into winds, His servants into flames of fire
views.case: The Hebrew word for messengers is the ordinary word for angels, and the Greek Old Testament reads it this way. The BSB footnote notes this reading, and Hebrews 1:7 quotes it in that form. On this view the verse is about the angels' nature, ever changing and active, which sets up the contrast with the Son.

views.label: The Hebrew allows both and the poet may have intended the ambiguity
views.case: Hebrew often leaves it open which of two nouns is the subject and which the predicate. The line may therefore hold both ideas together: the powers of nature and the servants of heaven are the same kind of thing in God's hand, His errand runners.

debates.bearing: Whichever way the grammar goes, the point is the same: both the forces of nature and the heavenly beings serve the LORD. Hebrews uses the Greek form to make a contrast with the Son.

debates.question: Are verses 6 to 9 about the third day of creation or about the flood?

views.label: The gathering of the waters at creation
views.case: The verses describe the waters standing above the earth, fleeing at God's rebuke, and mountains and valleys forming to a place He assigned. This matches Genesis 1:9-10, where the waters are gathered so that dry land appears. Verse 9's boundary then keeps the sea from covering the land.

views.label: The waters of Noah's flood
views.case: Verse 9 says the boundary is set 'that they may never again cover the earth,' which sounds like God's promise after the flood, Genesis 9:11. 'Never again' implies the waters once did cover the earth, and the psalm may be describing creation in the light of the flood and its limit.

views.label: Both are in view
views.case: Psalm 104 reads creation through Genesis as a whole. The phrase 'never again' can be heard as the covenant restraint that rests on the original ordering of the sea. Neither event is cut out of the picture, because the poet is interested in the standing fact that God holds the waters back.

debates.bearing: The point does not change. The sea has limits that God has set and keeps, and that is the ground for confidence in a world where water can destroy.

debates.question: How should a Christian read the wish in verse 35 that sinners vanish?

views.label: As an appeal for justice that God will end evil
views.case: The wish follows the picture of a world in order, and sin is the one thing that spoils it. Like Psalm 139:19, it asks God to remove what opposes Him. Evil is not the creature's fault in the same way as the lions and storms; it is rebellion, and the writer prays for its end.

views.label: As a prayer that sinners would be converted, not destroyed
views.case: God says He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but wants them to turn and live, Ezekiel 33:11, and 2 Peter 3:9 says He wants none to perish. Jesus calls His followers to pray for their enemies, Matthew 5:44. So the best way to pray verse 35 is for sin to be done away with, including in the one who prays.

views.label: As a human longing the psalm records honestly
views.case: The imprecatory strands of the Psalms show real emotion before God. The believer may pray them in a spirit informed by Christ, giving vengeance to God rather than taking it, and trusting His final justice, Revelation 21:1-5.

debates.bearing: The verse is a reminder that the goodness of creation has a shadow, and that a final answer to evil will have to come from God, not from us.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 4 turns on a word worth knowing. The Hebrew word for 'messengers' is malakh, which is the ordinary word for an angel as well as for a human envoy. Because 'winds' is the same word as 'spirits' (ruach), the line can be heard as either 'He makes the winds His messengers' or 'He makes His messengers winds.' The Greek Old Testament chose the second, and that is the form Hebrews 1:7 quotes, as the BSB footnote on this verse shows.

The word for God's 'chambers' in verse 3 is aliyyot, the upper rooms of a house, built on beams laid in the waters above. The poet pictures God's dwelling resting over the heavenly waters, and then in verse 13 the same word returns: 'He waters the mountains from His chambers.' So the rain on the hills comes from the upper rooms of God. The home and the weather are one picture.

In verse 7 the waters flee 'at Your rebuke.' The verb behind it, gaar, is the verb of a command given to something that has gone wrong, used of God rebuking nations and of Him rebuking the sea in Psalm 106:9, 'He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up.' The Gospels use the Greek counterpart when Jesus rebukes the wind and sea, Mark 4:39. The sea is not an enemy with its own will, only a servant that must be told to be still.

Verse 9 speaks of a 'boundary,' gevul, the term for a border marker between fields or nations. God surveys the sea as a landlord marks property. Job 38:10-11 and Jeremiah 5:22 use similar ideas of limits and barriers for the sea.

In verse 24 the works are made 'in wisdom,' chokhmah, the same wisdom that in Proverbs 3:19 'founded the earth,' and in Proverbs 8:30 is at God's side as a 'skilled craftsman.' Creation is not a heap but a well made thing, with order and skill built in.

A little joy-word links the psalm. In verse 15 wine 'gladdens' the heart, and in verse 31 the LORD 'rejoices' in His works. The Hebrew uses the root samach for both, and verse 34 uses it a third time: 'I rejoice in the LORD.' Divine joy, human gladness and the psalmist's worship are drawn from one root.

Verses 29 and 30 form a pair around ruach. When God 'takes away their breath,' creatures die; when He sends His 'Spirit' (the BSB footnote notes 'or breath'), they are created. The verb is bara, 'create,' the verb of Genesis 1:1, and the renewal is chadash, to make new. The same root appears in Isaiah 65:17, 'I will create new heavens and a new earth.' Finally, 'Hallelujah' in verse 35 is a command in the plural, 'praise the LORD' addressed to all, and it appears here for the first time in the Psalter.

typology.type: The Spirit who creates and renews, verse 30
typology.fulfillment: God sends His Spirit and creatures are created, and the face of the earth is renewed. The same Spirit hovered over the waters in Genesis 1:2. In the New Testament renewal becomes personal: God saved us 'through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,' Titus 3:5, and Paul writes that if anyone is in Christ he is 'a new creation,' 2 Corinthians 5:17. Jesus breathed on His disciples and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' John 20:22, an action that recalls the breath of life. The type is partial because the psalm speaks of creatures and soil; the Spirit in the New Testament renews hearts, and in the end the whole creation, Romans 8:21.

typology.type: The waters rebuked and held back, verses 6 to 9
typology.fulfillment: The sea that flees at God's rebuke finds its echo in the Gospels. Jesus rebukes the wind and sea and they obey, Mark 4:39, and the disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:41. He also walks on the sea, Matthew 14:25, doing what Job 9:8 says God alone does: 'treads on the waves of the sea.' The Gospels do not cite Psalm 104 explicitly, so this is an echo rather than a declared fulfilment, but the pattern is clear. The Creator who set the boundary of the sea is present among His creatures, and His disciples are slowly learning whose voice the waves obey.

typology.type: Bread, wine and oil from the earth, verses 14 and 15
typology.fulfillment: The gifts that sustain life and gladden the heart become signs in Jesus' ministry. At Cana He turns water into wine, John 2:7-10, and at the feeding of the crowd He gives thanks over the loaves and distributes them 'as much as they wanted,' John 6:11. At the Last Supper bread and wine become the signs of His body and blood, Matthew 26:26-28. The psalm sees the ordinary provisions of the world as gifts from God's hand; in Christ the same gifts point past themselves to the One who gives Himself as the food that satisfies. The correspondence rests on the gospel stories themselves, not on a New Testament citation of verse 15.

typology.type: The open hand that feeds every creature, verses 27 and 28
typology.fulfillment: Creatures look to God and He opens His hand. Jesus makes the same picture personal: the Father feeds the birds, and His children are worth more, Matthew 6:26 and Luke 12:24. In Christ the open hand reaches furthest, for 'He who did not spare His own Son' gives, and Paul says all things with Him, Romans 8:32. The type has limits: the psalm speaks of daily food, and the New Testament speaks of the gift of eternal life as the deeper feeding of the soul, John 6:35.

study.christ:
This psalm leads to Christ first by the claim that the world was made through Him. Colossians 1:16-17 says, 'For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible... All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.' John 1:3 says, 'Through Him all things were made.' If the psalm praises the One who stretches out the heavens like a tent and sets the earth on its foundations, the New Testament says that He did this through the Son. The one who stilled the waters at creation is the one who stilled them on the lake.

It leads to Christ again by the verb of keeping. Psalm 104 is not satisfied with a world that was made; it keeps saying that God sustains it. 'You open Your hand, they are satisfied' (verse 28). Hebrews 1:3 says the Son upholds 'all things by His powerful word,' and Colossians 1:17 that in Him all things hold together. John 5:17, 'To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working,' places Jesus inside the daily providence the psalm describes. The grass that grows and the lion that roars at night are held by the same hand that was nailed to a cross.

Hebrews 1:7 does a more particular thing. It quotes verse 4, in the Greek form, 'He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire,' to set the angels beside the Son. The angels are changeable servants. Of the Son the next verse says, 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever,' Hebrews 1:8. The psalm's own point, that the winds and flames are servants, lets the writer show that the Son is no servant of that kind.

The gospels show these themes in action. Jesus rebukes the sea, Mark 4:39. He walks on the waves, which Job 9:8 says God alone does. He feeds crowds from a few loaves, John 6:11, and turns water into wine, John 2:7-10. The disciples' question, 'Who is this?' Mark 4:41, is exactly the question the psalm prepares us to answer.

The Spirit of verse 30 points forward to Christ as well. The Spirit who renews the face of the earth is the Spirit Jesus breathes on His disciples, John 20:22, and the one poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior, Titus 3:6. The new creation that begins in Christ, 2 Corinthians 5:17, is the psalm's renewal reaching people.

A caution helps. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and we should not turn lions or cedars into pictures of Christ. The link is the New Testament's own: the One who made and keeps this world is the Son.
study.god:
The psalm gives a picture of God who is at once vast and near. He is 'very great,' clothed in splendor and majesty, wrapped in light as in a cloak, riding the clouds as a chariot (verses 1 to 3). Yet the same God gives drink to the wild donkey, plants the cedars, and makes grass grow for cattle. Nothing is too large for Him, and nothing too small.

He is wise. 'In wisdom You have made them all' (verse 24). The world is not a pile of accidents. The springs flow between mountains, the stork finds a home in the cypress, the rock badger a refuge in the cliff, the moon marks seasons and the sun knows when to set. Proverbs 3:19 says that the LORD founded the earth by wisdom, and Romans 1:20 says His eternal power and divine nature can be seen in what He made.

He is sovereign over the sea, over darkness, and over death. The waters flee at His rebuke, night comes at His word, and creatures die 'when You take away their breath' (verse 29). The psalm does not hide from mortality. It says plainly that life is a loan from God. Job 34:14-15 says the same: if He withdrew His breath, all flesh would perish together.

He is generous. Verse 27 says all creatures look to Him for food in season, and verse 28 that when He opens His hand 'they are satisfied with good things.' Even the young lions seek their food 'from God' (verse 21). Predator and prey both live from His hand, a thought that does not remove the hardness of the animal world but places it under His care. Matthew 5:45 adds that He sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous alike, and Acts 14:17 that He has not left Himself without witness, giving rain and food and gladness.

He is a God who delights. 'May the LORD rejoice in His works' (verse 31). Creation is not only a tool; it is a source of joy to Him, and Proverbs 8:30-31 pictures Him rejoicing in His whole world. Leviathan, the sea monster, is simply a creature He formed to play, which tells us that He is neither threatened nor ashamed of anything He made.

He is holy. The one discordant note is verse 35, and it reminds us that the Creator hates the evil that spoils His world. A God who delights in His works will not call evil good.

For worship, the psalm teaches that the first act of faith is to notice. Seeing the world as gift leads to praise. It also teaches that our praise lasts as long as our breath, and so, 'I will sing to the LORD all my life.'

crossReferences.note: The waters are gathered so that dry land can appear. Psalm 104:6 to 9 retells the same event as a scene of movement: waters standing over the mountains, fleeing at God's rebuke, and settling into the place He assigned. Reading the two together shows the psalm is expanding Genesis into a living picture.

God promises that never again will a flood destroy the earth. The psalm's boundary 'that they may never again cover the earth' (verse 9) echoes this covenant promise and shows creation held steady by God's word.

God asks Job who shut the sea behind doors and said, 'You may come this far, but no farther.' It is the same limit as Psalm 104:9, here put as a question that exposes human smallness and God's authority.

The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding. It gives the principle behind Psalm 104:24: the order of the world is the product of divine wisdom, never of accident or chance.
The eyes of all look to You, and You give them food in season; You open Your hand. This is almost word for word Psalm 104:27 and 28, so Israel was singing the same truth in more than one psalm.

Quotes verse 4 in its Greek form, 'He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire,' to show that angels are servants. The quote serves the argument that the Son is above them, because the Son is addressed as God.

All things were created through the Son and for Him, and in Him all things hold together. This is the New Testament's statement of who the Creator and Sustainer of Psalm 104 is, and of how He continues to hold the world.

God describes Leviathan as a beast no human can tame, and asks if Job can play with him as with a bird. Psalm 104:26 presents the same creature as a plaything for the LORD, which reverses the terror: what frightens us is small to Him.

Paul tells the Athenians that God gives everyone 'life and breath and everything else.' It is verses 27 to 30 carried to the Gentiles: the Creator needs nothing and sustains everything, and all people are His creatures.

Jesus points to birds that do not sow or reap and says the heavenly Father feeds them. It applies Psalm 104:27 and 28 to anxious disciples, with a conclusion the psalm only implies: if God feeds the birds, He will feed you.

The creation waits in eager expectation and groans like a woman in labor. It adds what Psalm 104 does not say: the renewal of the face of the earth is incomplete, and it awaits the revealing of the children of God.
The elders say, 'You created all things; by Your will they exist and came to be.' It turns Psalm 104's praise into heaven's worship, showing that the song of creation is sung at the throne.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with creation and ends with a new creation, and Psalm 104 is the place where the first is sung with full voice. After Genesis 1 told the story in the stately language of days, the psalm lets us feel what it is like to live in the world God made: light as a garment, springs in the valleys, birds in the branches, the work of the farmer and the sailor. It answers the question 'what kind of world is this?' with 'a world held in a generous hand.'

But the psalm is honest about shadows. Verse 29 says creatures die and return to dust, which is the sentence of Genesis 3:19. Verse 35 prays for sinners to vanish, an acknowledgement that something has gone wrong. The deep and the monster Leviathan remain in the background as reminders of chaos that God has leashed. The psalm celebrates creation in a world that is already fallen, and it keeps its praise in spite of that.

The story leans toward its rescue. The psalm says God sends His Spirit and creatures are made, and renews the face of the earth. That is a promise that creation will be remade, not abandoned. Isaiah 65:17 speaks of new heavens and a new earth, and Romans 8:19-22 says the creation will be 'set free from its bondage to decay.' Colossians 1:16-20 shows the means: the Son through whom everything was made is the one through whom God reconciles all things to Himself.

Its end is in Revelation 21 and 22. The sea that was a threat in the old order is gone, Revelation 21:1; the city needs no sun or moon because the glory of God lights it, Revelation 21:23; and the nations walk by its light. The cry of the psalm, 'May the LORD rejoice in His works,' is answered by a world fully His. The soul that began by blessing the LORD, and who wished for sin to vanish, finds in the new creation both wishes granted: evil is gone, and the praise can finally be complete.

sermon.title: The Pleasure of God in His Creation
sermon.why: Piper works directly through Psalm 104, especially verse 31, to show that God genuinely delights in what He has made, and that this pleasure is not idolatry but the overflow of the Father and Son's joy in each other, pressing the psalm's own movement from creation to worship of the Creator Himself.

quiz.q: What does the psalm say happens when God opens His hand toward His creatures, verses 27-28?

options.text: They gather what He gives and are satisfied with good things.
options.note: Every creature depends moment by moment on God's provision, not on its own securing of resources.

options.text: They immediately die and return to dust.
options.note: That describes the opposite scene, when God hides His face and takes away breath, verse 29.

options.text: They begin to build their own shelters.
options.note: The text is about receiving food from God's hand, not self-sufficient building.

options.text: They multiply beyond what the land can support.
options.note: Close to the theme of abundance, but the verse specifically names satisfaction with good things, not overpopulation.

quiz.q: According to verse 30, what renews the face of the ground?

options.text: God sending forth His Spirit.
options.note: The same Spirit active in Genesis 1:2 continually creates and renews; life and renewal come from God alone.

options.text: The changing of the seasons by human effort.
options.note: The verse credits God's Spirit, not human agricultural effort, with renewal.

options.text: The return of the rains after a drought.
options.note: Rain appears elsewhere in the psalm, but this verse specifically names God's Spirit as the source of renewal.

options.text: The migration of the animals to new habitats.
options.note: Animal habitats are described earlier in the psalm, but verse 30 is specifically about the Spirit renewing the ground.

quiz.q: What is Leviathan doing in the sea, according to verse 26?

options.text: Frolicking, formed by God to play there.
options.note: The psalm strips away the fear surrounding this creature, showing it as simply God's plaything in a sea fully under His rule.

options.text: Threatening to overwhelm the ships and destroy them.
options.note: The verse presents Leviathan as playful, not as a threat to shipping.

options.text: Hiding from the sun in the depths.
options.note: The text says Leviathan frolics, formed for that purpose by God, not that it is hiding.

options.text: Guarding the boundary between sea and land.
options.note: That boundary-setting role belongs to God Himself, verses 8-9, not to Leviathan.

quiz.q: What is the psalmist's resolve in verse 33?

options.text: To sing to the LORD all his life and sing praise to his God while he has his being.
options.note: The psalm moves from observing creation to a personal, lifelong vow of praise.

options.text: To catalog every species of creature he has observed.
options.note: The psalm has described many creatures, but verse 33 is a vow of praise, not a scientific resolve.

options.text: To build a temple in honor of creation.
options.note: No such building project is mentioned; the resolve is to sing and praise, not construct.

options.text: To retire from his work and rest permanently.
options.note: The psalm honors both labor and rest, verses 22-23, but verse 33's specific resolve is lifelong singing and praise.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament draw directly on this psalm to describe Christ?

options.text: Hebrews 1:7 quotes Psalm 104:4 to show the Son's supremacy over the angels who serve as winds and flames.
options.note: Hebrews 1 uses this very verse as part of its argument that the Son is worshipped, not merely one more servant like the angels.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: Hebrews 1:7 directly quotes this psalm, and Colossians 1:16-17 states the same truth of Christ sustaining all things.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of the new creation.
options.note: The psalm speaks of God's renewing Spirit and coming judgment on the wicked, not a specific date.

options.text: It is fulfilled only by modern advances in agriculture.
options.note: The psalm's deepest fulfillment is in Christ sustaining creation, Colossians 1:17, not in human technological progress alone.

questions: The psalm moves from the vastness of the heavens to God's minute care for badgers and birds. Where do you need to remember God's personal, detailed provision for you this week?
Verses 27 to 29 picture every creature waiting on God's open hand for its food and breath. What are you trying to secure for yourself that you actually need to receive from His hand instead?

The psalmist prays that his meditation would be pleasing to God and that he would rejoice in the LORD Himself, not merely in creation, verse 34. Are you enjoying God's gifts more than God Himself right now?
Verse 30 shows the Spirit renewing the face of the ground. Where in your own life, whether in weariness, sin, or grief, do you need that same renewing work of God's Spirit?

The psalm ends longing for sinners to vanish and the wicked to be no more, even in the middle of such wonder at creation. How does knowing creation itself groans for renewal, Romans 8:19-22, shape your hope for the brokenness you see in the world?

Piper's sermon notes that God delights in works no human eye will ever see, like creatures at the bottom of the sea. How does it change your prayer life to know that your private, unseen faithfulness is also seen and enjoyed by God?

translationNotes.note: The Septuagint renders this, He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire, the wording quoted in Hebrews 1:7; both readings show creation's forces obeying God's command as His servants.
Cypresses may also be rendered pines, junipers, or firs; the precise tree is uncertain in Hebrew, but the picture of God providing a safe habitat for the stork stands regardless.
Spirit can also be rendered breath; either way, the text credits God alone, not natural cycles, with creating and renewing life on the ground.
